reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its observable purpose is consumer guidance on obtaining Uber credits through referrals, cashback, discounted gift cards, and card benefits. The presenter discusses stated participation conditions, such as signing up with a code or using an eligible Visa card at participating businesses, without directing viewers to send money or private credentials to him. References to receipts, statement screenshots, promo-code searches, and discounted gift cards are presented as consumer advice, although the offers may not all remain current.

opening.argument: The video directly links free Uber value to actions viewers must take. It presents a referral path where someone signs up using the speaker’s code, and it advertises credits for that participation. It also directs viewers toward online promo-code searches and card-based activation and purchases. Framed together, this is not merely a description of rewards; it is a solicitation built around obtaining an unusually easy benefit through specific viewer actions. The promise is especially clear because the title itself foregrounds “FREE UBER Rides,” while the described steps require registration, spending, or supplying transaction evidence to claim the benefit.

the person who signs up using the code. Gets five dollars off their first four rides
All you have to do is use the Visa card. That is input into Uber's app

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling these ordinary rewards does not remove the promise-action structure. The defense itself identifies sign-up, referral-code use, and eligible-card use as conditions. Those are precisely the actions tied to the advertised credits. The fact that the speaker discusses several pathways, rather than requesting one payment, does not establish that the promised free rides are reliably available to viewers.

citations.quote: You can still give them your referral code
And you'll earn 5% back. In the form of Uber credits automatically

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited actions are ordinary eligibility conditions, not evidence of a deceptive claim. The referral offer is expressly limited: the code owner receives only a five-dollar credit, while the new user gets five dollars off each of four rides. The Visa benefit likewise requires using a card already entered in the app at participating businesses. These facts show a disclosed promotion tied to normal purchases, not an unsupported free-asset claim.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: the headline promises free rides, the narration mentions unusually large discounts, and some opportunities are described as easy to claim or available through unspecified online searches. The video says a $20 gift card may be sold for $10, that higher promo levels can reach $30, and that codes for existing users can occasionally be found. It also advises viewers to submit a receipt photo or card-statement screenshot when the credit fails to post. These combinations make the offer structure look more compelling than dependable: large returns, changing availability, external searches, and verification material are all used to sustain the promise of free Uber value.

20 ones even 30 ones

they normally ask you to provide a photo of your receipt

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats each item as an isolated consumer benefit and overlooks the cumulative presentation. The video encourages viewers to search online for codes whose destination is not specified, highlights discounts that may be limited, and still presents failed automatic credits as recoverable through submitted financial records. That combination supports concern about whether the promised benefit is as straightforward and broadly available as the presentation suggests.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are not hidden risk signals; the narration discloses the limitations. The speaker says the higher promo codes are only occasional, says the gift-card deals are normally limited to one per person, and recommends retaining receipts precisely because credits may not post automatically. A receipt or statement screenshot is evidence of a qualifying purchase, not a request for credentials or a payment to the speaker.

opening.argument: Although the video adopts the tone of practical credit-card guidance, its actual function is promotional: it repeatedly steers viewers toward referral participation, promo-code searches, card usage, gift-card purchases, and premium card benefits. The speaker calls one method a favorite, describes the combined return as “9% back,” and closes by asking viewers to subscribe and like the video. The educational framing therefore serves as a vehicle for promoting multiple ways to obtain the advertised free rides, while the title and description lead with free Uber value rather than neutral analysis.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls the material consumer guidance, but that is exactly the apparent role being used to make the offers persuasive. The video does not merely explain terms; it recommends specific participation routes, describes them as favorite or good deals, and ends with a channel-growth request. That promotional structure makes the free-ride promise the central call to action, not incidental background information.

citations.quote: Now this is one of my favorite ways. To earn free Uber credits

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A recommendation is not proof that the promotion is deceptive. The speaker gives concrete conditions and limits, including monthly expiration for one benefit, new-user restrictions, and the need to use participating businesses. The request to subscribe is a normal channel call to action and does not show that viewers are being induced to surrender money or credentials to obtain the credits.
